candidate.answerReason: Successive birthdays shift forward one weekday, or two when the interval includes February 29. Checking every year after 2008 gives the first Saturday in 2017.

methods.label: Track the weekday shifts
methods.explanation:
A year of \(365\) days contains \(52\) full weeks and one extra day, so the birthday usually moves forward one weekday. An interval containing February \(29\) has \(366\) days and moves it forward two weekdays.

May \(27\) comes after February \(29\), so the leap day of \(2008\) has already passed. The two-day shifts occur when moving into \(2012\) and \(2016\), the next leap years.

Starting from Tuesday in \(2008\), the birthdays fall on Wednesday in \(2009\), Thursday in \(2010\), Friday in \(2011\), and Sunday in \(2012\).

They then fall on Monday in \(2013\), Tuesday in \(2014\), Wednesday in \(2015\), Friday in \(2016\), and Saturday in \(2017\).

Every intervening year has been checked, so the next Saturday birthday is in \(2017\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
methods.levelReason: The solution uses calendar facts and remainders after complete seven-day weeks, without formal congruence notation.

candidate.annotationRationale: The assessed concept is seven-day remainder cycling: complete weeks leave the weekday unchanged. Calendar knowledge locates the leap days, and division-with-remainders meaning explains the one-day and two-day shifts.

review.mathematicalCheck: The successive shifts are one day except when crossing February 29 in 2012 and 2016. The birthdays from 2009 through 2017 are Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday, establishing the first return to Saturday.
review.levelCheck: Complete weeks and calendar facts provide an accessible AMC 10 explanation without formal congruence notation.
review.annotationCheck: Discarding complete weeks and adding the remaining weekday shifts instantiate remainder arithmetic. Calendar knowledge and division with remainders are appropriate supports.
